newsitem.title: INDIA: India checks wheat after Australia weed seeds find.
newsitem.headline: India checks wheat after Australia weed seeds find.

text.p: India has ordered authorities to ensure that wheat imports are free of weed seeds after some were found in shipments from Australia, local news agencies said on Sunday.

They said the Food Ministry will now require an additional declaration on the phytosanitary certificate assuring that wheat consignments are free of "exotic weeds" which could take root in India's wheat-growing areas, primarily in the north.
The Press Trust of India (PTI) said the declaration would be required for any new wheat import contracts.
"This is being discussed by the State Trading Corporation with Australian supplies and in the event of any difficulty in implementation, viable alternatives would be considered," PTI said.
Government officials could not be reached for confirmation.
Last week the Financial Express newspaper said the Agriculture Ministry had warned that recent imports of Australian wheat may have been contaminated.

The STC released a statement saying the entire quantity of 1.4 million tonnes of Australian wheat which had already arrived in India had been fully tested by the Australian Wheat Board before shipment and denied it was contaminated.
In December, India authorised STC to import two million tonnes of wheat to build stocks and check rising prices.
STC officials have said they had so far contracted to import 1.75 million tonnes, mainly from Australia, Argentina and Canada. STC has said the entire quantity had already arrived at Indian ports.
PTI and United News of India, quoting an Agriculture Ministry statement, said on Sunday that some weed seeds had been found in imported wheat.
They said the Food Corporation of India had been ordered to refrain from moving the imported wheat to any major wheat growing areas to prevent the weed seeds from entering Indian soil.
The distribution of wheat products would be permitted in wheat-growing areas only after the grain was milled near the ports of entry, they said.
The government ordered authorities to burn extraneous foreign matter including weed seeds, they said.
The government is considering sending experts to Australia to gain "first-hand information on the subject in the interest of smooth import operations in future", the news agencies said.
Last Tuesday, the STC said Indian plant protection and quarantine authorities had begun conducting pre-shipment inspections at loading ports in Australia.
